opus-5.5.text:
I think proliferation is one of the most important variables shaping the governance landscape, and it cuts in a few directions at once.

The basic dynamic is this: the cost of reaching a given level of capability falls over time, often quite steeply. Algorithmic progress, better hardware, distillation, and open-weight releases all push in the same direction. So whatever is at the frontier today, if you wait a year or two, many more actors can access something comparable. Frontier capabilities don't stay frontier. They diffuse.

That matters because most of our governance levers work best when the number of relevant actors is small. If only a handful of labs, in a handful of jurisdictions, can train or deploy a model with a particular dangerous capability, then you can imagine licensing, evaluations, safety standards, and international agreements doing a lot of work. You know who to talk to. You can verify things. Once that capability is available to thousands of actors, including ones who are anonymous or who don't care about your rules, many of those tools lose their grip.

So one way I frame it is that there's a window. For any given capability, there's a period when it's concentrated and therefore governable, followed by a period when it's diffused and governance has to shift toward resilience: hardening society, building defensive capabilities, adapting institutions. The strategic question is how to use the window well. Can we use the concentrated period to understand the risks, develop countermeasures, and put defenses in place before the capability is everywhere?

That leads to an offense-defense framing. For some capabilities, proliferation is basically fine or even good, because the defensive and beneficial uses dominate, and broad access spreads the benefits and avoids dangerous concentrations of power. For others, like meaningful uplift for biological weapons or certain cyber capabilities, the offense may dominate, at least for a while, and you'd want to slow diffusion while defenses catch up. A blanket "open everything" or "close everything" position misses that the answer depends on the capability and on where society's defenses stand.

There's also a real tension I want to be honest about. Restricting proliferation tends to concentrate power, in particular companies or governments, and concentration of power is itself one of the serious risks from advanced AI. So you're trading off misuse risk from diffusion against the risks of concentration and unaccountable control. Good governance has to take both seriously. That points toward institutions that keep frontier capability somewhat concentrated while making it accountable, transparent, and broadly beneficial, rather than just picking a side.

On the practical side, I think this is why compute has attracted so much attention. It's one of the few chokepoints that is physical, measurable, and concentrated in its supply chain, so it gives you some leverage over the pace and distribution of frontier development. But it doesn't solve the problem, because efficiency gains mean that over time you need less compute to reach a given capability.

So my overall view is that proliferation makes governance harder but not hopeless. It mainly changes the shape of the task. We need to govern the frontier while it's still governable, invest heavily in defensive and societal resilience for what will inevitably diffuse, and be thoughtful, capability by capability, about where diffusion is beneficial and where we should try to buy time.

r001.rationale: It names open-weight releases as one factor driving diffusion, but does not identify weight releases as probably the most significant source.

r002.rationale: It says costs fall steeply and more actors can access comparable capabilities over time, but does not describe training costs as declining exponentially.

r003.rationale: It says delayed models may be comparable to today’s frontier, not substantially inferior to it.

r004.rationale: It mentions developing defenses against risks generally, but does not describe using responsibly controlled frontier models to defend against misuse of inferior models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think proliferation is really one of the central variables here, and I'd break it down into a few pieces.

The first thing to say is that proliferation makes governance harder in a fairly direct way. If you have a world where frontier capabilities are concentrated in a small number of actors — say three or four labs, mostly in one or two jurisdictions — then in principle you have a tractable governance problem. You can have agreements among those actors, you can have regulators who know who to talk to, you can have norms around evaluation and deployment that are actually enforceable because there are few enough parties that defection is visible. Once capabilities are widely diffused — many companies, many countries, open-weight models that anyone can run and fine-tune — a lot of those levers just stop working. You can't regulate something that's in everyone's hands the way you can regulate something that lives in a handful of data centres.

But I think the picture is more nuanced than "concentration good, proliferation bad," for a couple of reasons.

One is that concentration carries its own risks. If a very small number of actors hold decisive capabilities, you have problems of accountability, of power concentration, of what happens if those actors have bad values or make mistakes. Historically, a lot of political thought is about how to prevent exactly that kind of concentration. So there's a real tension between the safety benefits of having few actors to coordinate and the legitimacy and robustness benefits of having many.

The second nuance is that it matters a lot what is proliferating. The capabilities that worry me most from a safety standpoint — things that could enable serious biological or cyber harms, or systems that are genuinely agentic and hard to control — those are the ones where I think the case for restricting diffusion is strongest. For a lot of other capabilities, broad access is probably net positive: more people can build defences, more researchers can study the systems, more of the world shares in the benefits. So I'd want to avoid talking about proliferation as one undifferentiated thing.

The third point is about the structure of the frontier over time. A lot of the governance arguments rely on there being a meaningful gap between the frontier and what's widely available. If that gap stays reasonably large — say the open or widely accessible models lag the frontier by a year or two — then you can do a lot of safety-relevant work at the frontier before capabilities diffuse. You have a window where you can evaluate, understand, and put mitigations in place. If the gap collapses, that window disappears, and governance has to be much more about resilience and defence than about controlling access.

So where does that leave me? I think the realistic picture is that some degree of proliferation is inevitable — the ideas and the hardware and the talent are too widely distributed to fully contain. The governance task, then, is less about preventing proliferation altogether and more about shaping it: trying to keep the most dangerous capabilities relatively contained, trying to preserve enough of a lead at the frontier that the actors there have time to do safety work, and investing heavily in societal resilience for the capabilities that will diffuse regardless. And a big part of that is international — the US and China and others reaching at least some shared understanding about what's truly off-limits, because unilateral restraint in a proliferating world doesn't buy you much.

I'd also say — and this is maybe the optimistic note — that proliferation isn't just a threat to governance, it's also a reason governance becomes more clearly necessary. When a capability is held by one actor, it's easy for everyone else to see the problem as "that actor's problem." When it's everyone's problem, you can sometimes get the kind of collective attention that makes real coordination possible. Whether we actually get there is the open question.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss exponentially declining training costs enabling more actors to acquire models of a given capability.

r003.rationale: It says accessible models might lag the frontier by a year or two, but does not observe that models diffusing with a two-year delay may be substantially inferior to the contemporary frontier.

r004.rationale: The response mentions building defenses and societal resilience broadly, but does not identify using responsibly controlled frontier models to defend against misuse of inferior models as a possible governance outcome.

astra-6.text:
I think proliferation makes the governance problem substantially harder, though it matters a lot what exactly is proliferating. Is it access to a model through an API? Is it the ability to download and modify the model? Or is it the expertise and infrastructure needed to build the next generation? Those give you quite different opportunities for oversight.

If the most dangerous capabilities are concentrated among a small number of actors, you at least have the possibility of agreeing on safety standards, monitoring compliance, and restricting particular uses. That doesn’t make those actors trustworthy, but it gives governance a more tractable target. If thousands of actors can independently produce or deploy those capabilities, an agreement among the leading labs becomes much less sufficient.

There are benefits to diffusion as well. You can get broader scrutiny, more people working on defensive applications, and less concentration of power. So I wouldn’t equate concentration with safety. The question is whether the benefits of wider access can be achieved without making especially dangerous capabilities effectively impossible to control.

One concern is that proliferation can be difficult to reverse. Once a model is widely available for people to run independently, discovering a serious vulnerability doesn’t mean you can recall it. That puts a premium on evaluating capabilities before release, and on distinguishing forms of access that preserve some ability to respond from forms that don’t.

So my overall view is that proliferation raises the demands on governance. We need institutions and safeguards that can keep working as the technology spreads, while being careful about decisions that remove our ability to intervene later.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss declining training costs or explain how they let more actors acquire models of a given capability.

r003.rationale: It does not compare delayed models with the contemporary frontier or mention a two-year delay.

r004.rationale: It mentions defensive applications in general, but does not describe responsibly controlled frontier models defending against misuse of inferior models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think proliferation makes the governance problem harder in several ways, although it matters a great deal what’s proliferating. Is it access to a model through an API? Is it the model weights? Or is it the ability to build the next generation of models? Those have quite different implications.

If the most dangerous capabilities are available to a large number of actors, then safety becomes less a matter of ensuring that a few organisations behave responsibly. You also need to worry about actors who are reckless, who have very different views about acceptable risk, or who actively want to cause harm. And once model weights have been widely distributed, it may be very difficult to withdraw a capability if you discover that it’s dangerous.

Proliferation can also make coordination harder. If there are a handful of actors at the frontier, you can at least imagine agreements on testing, security, and conditions for deployment. As the number grows, monitoring compliance and sustaining those agreements become more challenging.

But I wouldn’t conclude that the answer is simply to concentrate AI power as much as possible. Concentration creates its own serious risks: abuse of power, a lack of accountability, and potentially a very unequal distribution of the benefits. And wider access can help with research, scrutiny, and developing defences.

So the question I’d want us to ask is: how can we broadly share the benefits of AI while maintaining meaningful safeguards around capabilities that could cause very large harms? That requires being specific about the capability, the way it’s being shared, and whether the safeguards remain effective after it spreads.
